title: The Session Split

scenario.situation: A product team ran an A/B test on a new checkout flow. The experiment randomized by session and ran for two weeks. An analyst analyzed results at the user level and the p-value came back at 0.03 — just under the 0.05 threshold.
scenario.stakeholderBelief: The team is convinced the result is real and wants to ship the new checkout flow immediately.
scenario.question: Is the significant result trustworthy enough to ship on?

decisions.prompt: The team is ready to ship. How do you investigate whether this result is actually trustworthy?

options.label: Re-run the same user-level analysis with a stricter threshold
options.detail: Apply a Bonferroni correction or lower α to 0.01 and see if significance holds.
options.consequence: The result drops below significance at α=0.01, so you pump the brakes — but for the wrong reason. You haven't diagnosed why the original test was flawed; you've just raised the bar on a broken measurement.
options.divergenceCost: Tightened the threshold without questioning whether the test itself was structurally valid.

options.label: Audit the randomization and analysis unit alignment
options.detail: Check what unit the experiment randomized on, what unit the analysis ran on, and whether users appeared in both arms.
options.consequence: You immediately surface the mismatch: sessions were the randomization unit but users were the analysis unit. You can now check how many users spanned both arms — a concrete, falsifiable diagnostic that doesn't assume the result is right or wrong.

options.label: Check for novelty effect by looking at time-series conversion
options.detail: Plot daily conversion rates for both arms to see if the lift decays over the experiment window.
options.consequence: The time-series looks stable, so you conclude there's no novelty effect. But the real problem isn't a novelty effect — it's that the significance itself was manufactured by a unit mismatch. A clean time-series gives false reassurance.
options.divergenceCost: Investigated a real but secondary threat while the structural flaw went unexamined.

options.label: Validate by running a post-hoc power calculation
options.detail: Confirm the experiment was adequately powered for a user-level effect of the observed size.
options.consequence: The power calculation says you were well-powered — because it inherits the same inflated sample size from treating sessions as independent users. You've checked whether you had enough of the wrong unit.
options.divergenceCost: Validated the power of a misconfigured analysis, compounding the original error.

decisions.prompt: You pull the assignment logs. Which cut of the data best reveals whether the significance result should be trusted?

artifact.title: Sessions assigned per arm — 2-week experiment
artifact.caption: Session and user counts look balanced. But do the same users appear in both arms?

options.label: Session and user counts per arm
options.detail: Confirm both arms have roughly equal sessions and users to check for balance.
options.consequence: The arms look balanced — similar session counts, similar unique user counts. Nothing here raises a flag. But balance doesn't mean independence: it says nothing about whether the same users contributed sessions to both arms.
options.divergenceCost: Checked arm balance instead of arm contamination — confirmed the wrong property.

options.label: Share of users with sessions in both arms (contamination rate)
options.detail: Count users who appear in both control and treatment across their sessions.
options.consequence: The contamination rate is stark: 34% of users had sessions in both arms. Their repeated, correlated sessions were counted as independent observations, artificially deflating the standard error and producing a p-value that understates true uncertainty.

artifact.title: User assignment breakdown — contamination audit
artifact.caption: Over one-third of users spanned both arms. Their sessions were not independent observations — the effective sample size, and therefore the p-value, is invalid.

decisions.prompt: You've shown that 34% of users were contaminated across both arms. What do you tell the team?

options.label: "The experiment is invalid — the new checkout flow has no real effect."
options.detail: Tell the team the result is false and there is no lift.
options.consequence: You've overcorrected. Contamination invalidates the inference but doesn't prove the null — the new checkout flow might still have a real effect. Declaring no effect is as unjustified as shipping on the original p-value.
options.divergenceCost: Overclaimed in the opposite direction — declared the null from a flawed test.

options.label: "The p=0.03 result is unreliable due to a randomization-analysis unit mismatch — we can't ship on it. We should re-run the experiment randomized by user to get a valid inference."
options.detail: Explain the structural flaw, its mechanical effect on variance, and recommend a correctly designed re-run.
options.consequence: You've separated what the data can and cannot say. The team understands why the result is untrustworthy, what specifically needs to change, and has a concrete path to a valid answer. That's the right outcome from a broken experiment.

insight: The significance was an artifact of a unit mismatch: randomizing by session but analyzing by user meant correlated sessions from the same user were treated as independent observations, understating variance and shrinking the p-value artificially. Over a third of users contaminated both arms, making the effective sample size far smaller than the session count implied. The lesson is precise: you must randomize and analyze at the same unit — any mismatch breaks the independence assumption that frequentist inference depends on, and no amount of threshold-tightening or power-checking will catch it.
